newsitem.title: UK: UK's Lang announces plans to curb public strikes.
newsitem.headline: UK's Lang announces plans to curb public strikes.

text.p: British Trade and Industry Secretary Ian Lang on Wednesday announced plans to allow people affected by strikes in monopoly public services to sue the trade union involved for damages.

"We're going to bring out a consultation paper very soon. It's going to include a package of measures of which this is just one," Lang told BBC radio during the ruling Conservative Party's annual conference.

He was immediately accused of "union bashing" by Alan Johnson, joint general secretary of the Communication Workers Union representing postal workers, who have called several one-day strikes this year as part of a dispute over conditions.
Johnson told the BBC that the government wanted to demonise workers in essential industries and the plans would effectively be to ban strikes in key public services.

But Lang denied the charge, saying: "We're not contemplating a ban on...strikes in certain services, what we're doing is looking at this from the point of view of the public and the effect this has on them."
Since taking power in 1979 the Conservatives have passed a series of laws severely clipping the powers of the once mighty trade unions.
"We're not banning strikes, what we're saying to people is this, this is one more hurdle, this is a risk that you will have to assess before you take action," Lang said.
"Therefore you will have to be that much more responsible when bringing third parties into a dispute by putting them at your mercy, leaving them without a service."

Asked whether the current postal strike could be the sort of action which would allow a company to sue for damage to its business, Lang said: "That would depend on the degree to which your business had suffered."
